implementation_notes: In Node.js a synchronous `if (seen.has(key)) return; seen.add(key);` block is atomic with respect to other event-loop turns - provided no await sits between the check and the add - so a Map/Set replaces the classic store for single-process receivers. It survives neither cluster workers, nor several pods, nor a process recycle, so production receivers whose duplicates can outlive the process use the Redis claim below or a SQL claim. Retention is manual: store an expiry with each key and sweep on a timer, because Map entries never expire.
pitfalls: An await between the existence check and the insert in the in-process guard reopens the race: other event-loop turns interleave.
cluster workers and worker_threads each own their Set, so the guard must move to Redis or a database to protect a fleet.
Map/Set entries never expire on their own; sweeping only while traffic arrives leaves stale keys behind on a quiet queue.

variants.name: Distributed claim with Redis SET NX PX
variants.implementation_notes: `SET key 1 NX PX <ttl>` is a single-command compare-and-set: it returns OK only for the first caller, so one round trip both claims the key and arms its expiry - the standard distributed claim behind several Node processes. A null reply means duplicate; a connection error must be treated as retryable, never as duplicate. Size the TTL to the broker's redelivery window and keep the key in a namespace per consumer group when several subscribers share the store.
pitfalls: A failed Redis call must not be mapped to 'duplicate': only the conditional-set result distinguishes the cases, errors must propagate for redelivery.
NX keys expire on their own, so a retention shorter than the redelivery window silently reopens duplicates; longer retention merely costs memory.
